newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM says Kabila recognition likely.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM says Kabila recognition likely.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Monday that Japan, a major importer of metals from Zaire, was likely to recognise the new government of rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
"Although we have to consult with the Foreign Ministry, I think we will recognise it," Hashimoto told reporters. "I hope it will swiftly restore peace so that racial conflict does not intensify."
Kabila, chairman of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), proclaimed himself head of state on Saturday, ousting long-ruling president Mobutu Sese Seko.
Japan's imports of cobalt from Zaire totalled 1,533 tonnes in calendar 1996, roughly 30 percent of its total imports of the strategic metal.
In another comment, top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters Japan wanted "Kabila and his new government to present clear-cut ways to shift into democracy."
Kajiyama also called on Kabila's government to respect human rights and deal with Zaire's hundreds of thousands of refugees "in a humanitarian way".

Earlier this month, Japan opened its first formal contact with Kabila when envoy Ryuichi Shoji, director of the Foreign Ministry's Africa division, met the rebel leader in Goma as he prepared for a final advance on Zaire's capital of Kinshasa.
Kabila's takeover of Zaire coincides with a push by the Japanese government for a higher profile in Africa.
On his return from the Zaire mission, Shoji told Reuters Japan planned to put more effort into its relations with African nations.
"Japan has no colonial past in Africa and that can be a political advantage in helping us to settle problems there," Shoji said.

The Trade Ministry said Japan's exports to Africa were $5.71 billion in calendar 1996, accounting for only 1.3 percent of the total, while imports from the continent were $4.97 billion, or 1.4 percent of the total.
Japan's largest trading partner in Africa is South Africa, with exports totalling $2.06 billion and imports worth $2.82 billion in 1996.
